title: THERE WAS POISON IN THE STEW. ELISHA THREW FLOUR INTO THE POT.
paragraphs: THERE WAS POISON IN THE STEW. ELISHA THREW FLOUR INTO THE POT.

They were already hungry. Then the meal meant to keep them alive became the thing that could kill them. And somewhere inside this strange Old Testament miracle is a terrifying question for every Christian: What happens when death gets into something you thought was feeding you?
“Death is in the pot.”
Four words.
But imagine hearing them when you are already starving.
Not sitting comfortably at a table with another meal waiting in the refrigerator. Not debating theology with a full stomach. Not reading the story from the safety of thousands of years later.
There was famine.
Real famine.
The kind that makes people look at ordinary food differently. The kind that makes whatever you can find in a field feel like mercy.
Second Kings 4:38 tells us that Elisha had returned to Gilgal and “there was a famine in the land.”
The sons of the prophets were gathered before him.
Hungry men.
A hungry land.
An empty stomach has a way of making almost anything look edible.
So Elisha gave the instruction: put on the large pot. Make stew for the sons of the prophets.
You can almost hear the fire crackling underneath it.
Someone went into the field searching for something to contribute. He found a wild vine. He gathered wild gourds until his garment was full, brought them back, sliced them into the stew...
and Scripture quietly adds the sentence upon which the whole disaster turns:
כִּי־לֹא יָדָעוּ
Ki lo yada'u.
“For they did not know.”
They did not know what they were putting into the pot.
That sentence should frighten us more than it does.
Because some of the most destructive things that enter a life do not arrive wearing a sign that says POISON.
Sometimes they look useful.
Sometimes they look harmless.
Sometimes everybody else seems comfortable with them.
Sometimes they are introduced by someone who genuinely believes he is helping.
The man gathering the gourds was not presented as an enemy.
He was trying to feed hungry people.
There is no indication in the passage that he deliberately poisoned anyone.
He simply did not know.
And ignorance did not make the danger harmless.
That reaches painfully into our generation.
Not everything poisoning us was invited into our lives because we wanted rebellion.
Some things entered because we were hungry.
Hungry for love.
Hungry to belong.
Hungry to stop feeling lonely.
Hungry for somebody to tell us we mattered.
Hungry for success.
Hungry for attention.
Hungry for relief.
Hungry for affection.
Hungry for answers.
Hungry for something—anything—that would quiet the ache inside us.
And hunger can make dangerous things look nourishing.
Maybe that relationship looked like love.
Maybe that compromise looked like survival.
Maybe bitterness initially felt like protection.
Maybe pornography promised comfort and became bondage.
Maybe pride disguised itself as confidence.
Maybe greed called itself ambition.
Maybe gossip disguised itself as concern.
Maybe unforgiveness felt like justice.
Maybe spiritual laziness became “I’m just tired.”
Maybe slowly drifting from Scripture felt harmless because you still believed in God.
Maybe nobody noticed.
Maybe you did not notice.
Until one day you tasted what your life had become and something inside you finally screamed:
There is death in this pot.
The Hebrew is brutally short:
מָוֶת בַּסִּיר
Mavet bas-sir.
“Death in the pot.”
Not inconvenience.
Not disappointment.
Death.
The men could not continue eating.
And there are moments when grace begins precisely there—when God finally allows us to recognize that something we have been consuming cannot keep being consumed.
There comes a moment when pretending becomes more painful than confession.
A moment when the Christian vocabulary cannot hide the private decay anymore.
A moment when Sunday worship cannot silence what Monday through Saturday has become.
A moment when you realize you have been asking God to bless something He has been calling you to surrender.
Maybe you know that moment.
The browser closes.
The argument ends.
The bottle is empty.
The message has already been sent.
The room becomes quiet.
Everybody else is asleep.
And suddenly there is nowhere left to run from yourself.
You whisper what you have been afraid to admit:
“Lord... something is wrong with me.”
But listen carefully.
That is not necessarily the sound of God abandoning you.
Sometimes that is the sound of mercy waking you up.
Because the men in 2 Kings 4 did something incredibly important.
They cried out.
They did not quietly keep eating because they were embarrassed.
They did not pretend the stew was fine because somebody might be offended.
They did not say, “Well, everybody has their own truth about what is in the pot.”
They recognized danger and cried:
“Man of God, there is death in the pot!”
Somebody reading this needs permission to finally say it.
There is death in my pot.
There is something in my marriage that cannot remain hidden.
There is something happening inside my mind that I need help with.
There is resentment in me.
There is lust in me.
There is pride in me.
There is jealousy in me.
There is secret compromise in me.
There is an addiction I keep renaming so I do not have to confront it.
There is a wound I turned into an identity.
There is a sin I have been managing instead of confessing.
There is a version of Christianity I have constructed where Jesus is allowed to comfort me but never command me.
There is death in the pot.
And then Elisha does something strange.
He does not throw away the people.
He addresses the pot.
“Bring flour.”
The Hebrew word is:
קֶמַח
Qemach.
Flour.
Second Kings 4:41 records:
וּקְחוּ־קֶמַח
Uqehu-qemach.
“Bring flour.”
Elisha threw the flour into the pot and told them to serve the stew again.
Then Scripture gives the astonishing conclusion:
וְלֹא הָיָה דָּבָר רָע בַּסִּיר
Ve-lo hayah davar ra bas-sir.
“There was no harmful thing in the pot.”
The danger was gone.
We should be careful here.
The Bible does not explicitly tell us that the flour was a symbol of Jesus Christ. We should never force Scripture to say something it does not say merely because it makes a dramatic sermon.
The miracle belongs to God.
Flour was the means Elisha was instructed to use in the narrative, but flour itself is not presented as magical. The point is the intervention and provision of the God Elisha served.
And yet, when Christians read this event within the whole story of Scripture, something larger comes into view.
Because humanity has a far greater problem than poisoned stew.
Death entered our world through sin.
Romans tells us that “the wages of sin is death.”
We did not merely need moral improvement.
We needed rescue.
We needed reconciliation.
We needed forgiveness.
We needed life.
And God did not stand at a safe distance from our ruin.
Jesus Christ came into it.
The eternal Son took on flesh.
He walked among sinners.
He touched lepers.
He welcomed the despised.
He confronted hypocrites.
He ate with people respectable society had written off.
He called sinners to repentance.
He carried the cross.
And at Calvary, the One who had no sin bore our sins in His body.
The scandal of Christianity is not that good people can become slightly better.
It is that guilty people can be forgiven because Jesus Christ died and rose again.
That is scandalous grace.
The cross does not pretend the poison was harmless.
The cross proves how deadly sin actually is.
Grace does not say your rebellion did not matter.
Grace says it mattered so much that redemption cost the blood of Christ.
And resurrection announces that death does not get the final word.
That is why repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you away from the pot that is killing you.
Jesus did not begin His public proclamation by telling humanity to become more comfortable with its poison.
“Repent, and believe in the gospel.”
Turn.
Come home.
Stop defending what is destroying you.
Stop decorating the prison.
Stop calling chains jewelry.
Stop demanding that Jesus approve the very thing from which He came to save you.
And perhaps the hardest sentence in this entire article is this:
You cannot ask Jesus to save you while insisting that He never confront you.
He loves you too much for that.
Some people want a Savior who rescues them from consequences but never challenges their desires.
But biblical grace is more beautiful than that.
Jesus forgives.
Jesus cleanses.
Jesus restores.
Jesus also transforms.
The Gospel does not merely give you a cleaner record.
Christ gives you a new life.
And maybe this is where your story changes.
Not when everybody finally understands you.
Not when every wound disappears overnight.
Not when temptation stops knocking.
Not when your past magically becomes less painful.
Maybe your story begins changing when you stop hiding the poison.
When you finally tell Jesus the truth He already knows.
When confession becomes more important than reputation.
When repentance becomes more precious than appearances.
When you stop saying, “This is just who I am,” and begin asking, “Jesus, who are You calling me to become?”
There is something deeply moving about those hungry prophets eating again.
Think about it.
Minutes earlier they believed the meal contained death.
Then God intervened through His prophet, and the food that could not be eaten was served again.
Fear gave way to provision.
The table that had become a place of terror became a place where hungry people could eat.
God did not merely expose what was wrong.
He demonstrated His power over it.
And perhaps you need to hear this tonight:
Exposure is not always the end of your story.
What if the thing you are most ashamed for God to uncover becomes the very place where you discover how deep His mercy runs?
Peter denied Jesus.
Three times.
The disciple who had boasted that he would never fall collapsed spectacularly when pressure came.
But the resurrected Christ did not discard Peter.
Jesus restored him.
That does not make Peter's denial acceptable.
It makes Christ's grace astonishing.
The woman caught in adultery encountered mercy, but mercy did not rename sin as righteousness. Jesus told her to leave her life of sin.
The thief dying beside Christ had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
He had nothing impressive to offer.
He turned toward Jesus.
And Jesus gave a dying criminal hope beyond the grave.
This is the Gospel.
Not pretending poison is food.
Not pretending sin is harmless.
Not pretending judgment is imaginary.
Not pretending we can rescue ourselves.
The Gospel tells the devastating truth about us and then announces the breathtaking truth about Christ.
We sinned.
Christ came.
Christ died.
Christ rose.
Christ saves.
Christ forgives.
Christ restores.
Christ transforms.
And nobody is beyond the reach of His grace who truly comes to Him.
Maybe there has been poison in your pot for years.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you learned how to smile while dying inside.
Maybe you learned Christian language well enough to keep people from asking deeper questions.
Maybe your Bible is highlighted while your heart is exhausted.
Maybe you worship publicly and weep privately.
Maybe you keep promising God, “This is the last time.”
Then there is another last time.
And another.
And another.
Until shame whispers that Jesus must finally be tired of you.
Do not confuse the voice of shame with the call of Christ.
Shame tells you to hide.
Jesus calls you into the light.
Shame tells you there is no way home.
Jesus says, “Come to Me.”
Shame tells you your scandal has become your identity.
The Gospel tells you that for those who belong to Christ, sin does not get to write the final chapter.
Bring it into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Ask for help.
Open Scripture again.
Pray even if your prayer comes out broken.
Find mature believers who will tell you truth instead of merely telling you what feels good.
If you have fallen, do not make a home on the ground.
Run to Christ.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you feel worthy.
Now.
Because you were never saved by being worthy.
You are saved by grace through faith.
And grace is not permission to remain comfortably in sin.
Grace teaches us to say no to ungodliness and to live for God.
That is transformation.
Not because scandal becomes beautiful.
Because Jesus rewrites what sin tried to destroy.
Maybe your family only remembers what you did.
Jesus knows what His grace can make of you.
Maybe people still introduce you by your worst chapter.
Jesus knows the chapters that have not been written yet.
Maybe your own mind keeps replaying the person you used to be.
But if anyone is in Christ, Scripture says there is new creation.
The old has passed away.
The new has come.
And that means your testimony does not have to be, “I never had poison in the pot.”
Your testimony can be:
“There was death in the pot...
but God met me there.”
If this exposed something you have been hiding, do not write an essay explaining yourself. You do not owe strangers your private details.
Let somebody know there is a real person behind the screen who is still reaching toward Jesus.
Your testimony may become somebody else's reason not to give up tonight.
Not because every sentence will feel equally powerful tomorrow, but because there may come a night when the old poison starts looking attractive again.
Come back and remember.
Hunger does not make poison food.
Temptation does not make sin safe.
Failure does not make Christ powerless.
And shame does not get the final word over a repentant sinner who runs to Jesus.
Not merely because Gospel Warrior needs another share.
Send it privately to the person you cannot stop thinking about while reading this.

And invite your family, your church friends, the believer who has drifted, the person questioning everything, the lukewarm Christian, and even the unbeliever who thinks Christianity is only about religious people pretending to be good.
Let them see what the Gospel actually says.
We were not good enough.
Jesus was.
We could not pay our debt.
Jesus did.
Death appeared to have won on Friday.
The tomb was empty on Sunday.

If you sincerely want your resources to glorify God, one practical way to participate is to help sustain the work that carries His Word outward. Salvation cannot be bought, and giving does not make anyone more loved by Christ. We support Gospel work because grace has already been freely given to us.
And comment—even if all you can manage tonight is:
“Jesus, forgive me.”
Because perhaps the most dangerous moment was never discovering there was death in the pot.
Perhaps it would have been discovering it...
and continuing to eat.
Christ did not come merely to make poisoned lives more tolerable.
He came that sinners might repent, be forgiven, reconciled to God, and receive life in His name.
The poison may explain part of your story. It does not have the authority to write your ending when Jesus Christ becomes Lord of it.
